label: Person
name: Diotimus the Stoic
summary:
Diotimus the Stoic, active around 100 BCE, was a Hellenistic philosopher primarily known for his polemical attacks against the Epicurean school and his contributions to Stoic ethical thought. Operating within the vibrant intellectual milieu of the late Roman Republic, his writings reflect the ongoing philosophical rivalries that characterized the period, particularly the Stoic-Epicurean debate over the nature of pleasure, virtue, and the highest good. Though his own works are lost, his arguments and accusations were preserved by later doxographers, providing valuable, if biased, insight into the philosophical controversies of the era and the intellectual strategies employed by competing schools.

Diotimus gained particular notoriety for his accusation that Epicurus had plagiarized the doctrines of Democritus, specifically regarding atomism, and those of Aristippus of Cyrene concerning the concept of pleasure as the ultimate good. He allegedly authored a work titled *Against Epicurus*, which detailed these charges, aiming to undermine the originality and intellectual integrity of the Epicurean school. This strategy positioned Stoicism as the more authentic and rigorous philosophical tradition. Beyond these attacks, Diotimus also engaged with core Stoic tenets, likely elaborating on concepts such as *oikeiôsis* (appropriation) or the role of reason in achieving *eudaimonia* (flourishing), though the specifics of these contributions are largely lost.
